phonemes.desc: Voiced labiodental fricative [v], as in English 'vine'.
Short open-mid front [ɛ], the reduced vowel of the first syllable.
Voiced lateral l, short [ɛ], voiceless s; the name's deeper etymology is one of the open problems of Slavic philology.

pronunciation.approximation: 'VEH-les', two quick syllables; the stress falls forward, as in the modern South Slavic reflexes of the name.

domains.title: Veles
domains.subtitle: Cattle
domains.lead: Veles — Volos to the East Slavs — is the god of cattle and wealth, of the underworld's moist depths, and, in the great reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, of poetry and magic. Where Perun strikes from above, Veles moves below: through herds, graves, bargains, and song.

cards.name: Lord of Cattle
cards.desc: The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore their oaths by him alone.

cards.name: The Underworld River
cards.desc: He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm of the dead and of hidden treasure.

cards.name: God of Poetry
cards.desc: In the reconstructed mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name.

cards.name: Adversary of Perun
cards.desc: The eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down each spring by the thunderer's bolt.

symbols.name: Cattle horns
symbols.meaning: The herds that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore

symbols.name: The serpent
symbols.meaning: His disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of the eagle

symbols.name: The bear
symbols.meaning: His chthonic animal in the alternating lore of the Slavic year — master of the wilderness beyond the fence

symbols.name: Gusli (harp)
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the singer he protects; in folklore the magic fiddle makes even the forest dance

symbols.name: Wet earth and roots
symbols.meaning: The moist underworld into which he withdraws and from which wealth returns

mythology.lead: Veles has no surviving epic. His dossier is a chronicle oath here, a famine there, and — towering over the fragments — the modern reconstruction by Ivanov and Toporov of the myth-cycle in which he is the thunderer's eternal adversary. Read together, the fragments describe a god of everything that grows, burrows, and accrues out of sight.

myths.title: Sworn by Volos
myths.text: The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the only verbatim ritual text of pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and the curse on the perjurer is total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our shields, may we be slain by our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the cattle god.' The division of labor is the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where your property lives, there your god is invoked.

myths.title: The Angry God of Suzdal
myths.text: In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The volkhvy demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, from a particular kin — and when the killing was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still Veles whose name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained hunger.

myths.title: The Theft of the Cattle
myths.text: In the reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, Slavic mythology's central cycle runs like this: Veles, dwelling in the underworld beneath the world-tree, commits a crime against the sky — he steals Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his bride. Perun descends in pursuit, hurling his bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. No East Slavic manuscript tells this story; it survives in the pairing of the gods in the treaty oaths, in wedding laments where the bride weeps for a brother struck or drowned, in South Slavic spring songs, and in the universal Indo-European pattern of the storm-god and the serpent. The scholars who built it were explicit that they were reconstructing — and the pieces fit with a stubbornness no rival hypothesis has matched.

myths.title: Volos's Street
myths.text: Novgorod kept Veles in its very street plan. Birchbark letters of the eleventh and twelfth centuries — mundane shopping lists and debt notes scratched by ordinary citizens — give addresses on Volosova ulica, 'Volos's street', the commercial quarter by the market. No chronicle mentions it; the god's presence in the townscape was simply assumed, a neighborhood named for him the way others were named for craftsmen. When we read a debtor promise to pay on Volos's street, we watch the cult outliving the conversion in the least sacred of registers: commerce. Perun got treaties, curses, and weeping crowds; Veles got the marketplace — which may be the more honest monument, since people swore by the thunderer but they lived by the herder. A street, unlike a statue, has to be used to survive — and Volosova ulica was used every market day for a hundred years after the gods went under.

lore.syncretism: Veles's Christian afterlife ran through the saints of the herd. In the Balkans he survives in Sveti Vlaho — Saint Blaise — the Dalmatian patron of cattle whose feast ends with animals blessed in his name; in Russia the same role fell to Saint Vlasiy, whose name is simply Veles re-clothed. The divine adversary was absorbed too: the serpent of the myth-cycle slithered into dragon-slayer legends, and Perun's spring victory was reassigned to Saint George and Elijah. Byzantine-educated writers performed interpretatio on the pantheon as a whole, while comparative scholarship drew bolder lines — Toporov's Veles–Varuna, the Norse Óðinn of poetry and the dead, Hermes as god of herds and boundary-crossings — each a hypothesis about what sort of god this was: sovereign of everything the sky does not see. Demonized in the languages (Czech veles gave way to čert for 'devil'), he remained the underworld's landlord in folklore down to the modern era.
lore.culturalLegacy: Veles endures most durably in words: toponyms like Volosovo across the Russian north, the Dalmatian cult of Sveti Vlaho, the devil-haunted velnias of Lithuanian folklore, and the root itself in Slavic speech. Folklore kept his portfolio — treasure guarded by a chthonic serpent, the magic fiddle of the singer who bargains below, oaths sworn over a herd at market. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries were less kind: the so-called Book of Veles, publicized in the 1950s, purports to be a pre-Christian epic of his people and is now universally judged a modern forgery — a tribute, of a crooked kind, to how badly moderns wanted the lost god back. Rodnover communities today honor Veles as lord of wisdom, wealth, and the written word, and his serpent still guards vaults in banks' logos and fantasy novels alike.
lore.extendedMeditation: Veles is the god of the other economy. Perun owns everything visible — the strike, the oath, the battle won — but Veles owns what accumulates quietly: calves, coins, verses, graves. He is the patron of everyone who works below the threshold of glory: the herder, the merchant, the poet, the sorcerer, the dead. His mythology, reconstructed stitch by stitch by modern scholars, tells of a being who is defeated every spring and never finally destroyed — which is exactly the biography of wealth, and of life itself returning from underground. There is something subversive in his survival. The chronicles drown his sorcerers in the Volga, demonize his name, and reassign his cattle to Saint Blaise; and meanwhile ordinary Novgorodians keep doing business on his street, in writing, for centuries. Veles teaches that the underworld is not the opposite of prosperity but its storehouse: everything valuable is buried for a season, and the god of the deep is the one who remembers where.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Veles has been identified, and his material dossier is thin — fitting for a god of hidden things. The anchor is textual-archaeological: birchbark letters from eleventh–twelfth-century Novgorod address creditors and debtors on Volosova ulica, 'Volos's street', the market quarter — proof that the cult left footprints in urban topography even where no shrine survives. Riverside hoards and water-logged deposits are sometimes laid at the door of the underworld god, but the attribution is unprovable, and no figurine or amulet bears his name. The honest summary is that Veles's archaeology is his absence: the god of concealment kept himself concealed, and the street sign is the whole monument.
